chapter.title: Everyday .NET
chapter.para: .NET's class library is large, documented, and the same on every system. These recipes use the parts a Rexx program needs most: dates, text, numbers, files, regular expressions, JSON and hashes.

section.title: Dates and Times
section.para: You want to compute with dates, and to show them in any language.

example.title: Dates and Times
example.programlisting:
dt = .net~System~DateTime d = dt~new(2026, 10, 16, 15, 30, 0) say d~ToString("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm") "is a" d~DayOfWeek say "In 100 days:" d~AddDays(100)~ToString("dddd, d MMMM yyyy") say "Until 2027:" dt~new(2027, 1, 1)~Subtract(d)~TotalDays~format(, 2) "days" span = .net~System~TimeSpan~FromSeconds(3725) say "3725 s =" span~Hours"h" span~Minutes"m" span~Seconds"s" es = .net~System~Globalization~CultureInfo~GetCultureInfo("es-ES") say d~ToString("D", es) p = dt~ParseExact("16/10/2026", "dd/MM/yyyy", .net~System~Globalization~CultureInfo~InvariantCulture) say p~Year p~Month p~Day p~DayOfYear
::requires "net.cls"
example.screen: 2026-10-16 15:30 is a Friday In 100 days: Sunday, 24 January 2027 Until 2027: 76.35 days 3725 s = 1h 2m 5s viernes, 16 de octubre de 2026 2026 10 16 289

section.para: How it works. A DateTime is made from its parts, or parsed (ParseExact with a format, culture-invariant). Its methods return new values (AddDays, Subtract, which gives a TimeSpan), and ToString formats it, in the current culture or in the one given: CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo("es-ES") for Spanish. DayOfWeek is an enum value, which shows its name. DateTime is a struct: what Rexx holds is a copy.
See also Reference, Values, Messages to Types and Objects.

section.title: Formatting Text
section.para: You want to format numbers and text as .NET does.

example.title: Formatting Text
example.programlisting:
s = .net~System~String say s~Format("{0,-6}|{1,6}|", "left", "right") say s~Format("{0:N2} {1:N2}", 1234.5, .net~double(1234.5)) -- a Rexx string is a string inv = .net~System~Globalization~CultureInfo~InvariantCulture de = .net~System~Globalization~CultureInfo~GetCultureInfo("de-DE") n = .net~double(1234567.891) say s~Format(inv, "{0:N2}", n) "/" s~Format(de, "{0:N2}", n) say n~class~id .net~double(5)~string say inv~TextInfo~ToTitleCase("the quick brown fox") say s~Join(", ", .array~of("a", "b", "c"))
::requires "net.cls"
example.screen: left | right| 1234.5 1,234.50 1,234,567.89 / 1.234.567,89 NETTYPED a System.Double (5) The Quick Brown Fox a, b, c

section.para: How it works. String.Format takes .NET's composite formats: alignment ({0,-6}) and number formats ({0:N2}). A format applies to a number, and a Rexx string is a string: 1234.5 goes to Format's object parameters as the string "1234.5", which N2 leaves alone. .net~double(x) makes it a double, which N2 formats; it is only a mark for the call (a NetTyped), not a number of its own. A culture as the first argument formats in that culture's way.
See also Reference, Values, Forcing a Type.

section.title: Big Integers and Decimals
section.para: You want integers of any size, or decimal arithmetic, from .NET.

example.title: Big Integers and Decimals
example.programlisting:
bi = .net~System~Numerics~BigInteger f = bi~One do i = 2 to 30; f = bi~Multiply(f, i); end -- Rexx numbers go as BigIntegers say "30! =" f~ToString big = bi~Pow(2, 200)~ToString say "2**200 has" big~length "digits:" big~left(20)"..." numeric digits 70 say "In Rexx:" bi~Parse(big)~ToString / 2**190 d = .net~System~Decimal say d~Divide(1, 3) d~Round(d~Divide(2, 3), 4)
::requires "net.cls"

section.para: How it works. System.Numerics.BigInteger has no size limit. A Rexx whole number goes to a BigInteger parameter exactly, with all its digits; a BigInteger comes to Rexx as a NetObject, whose ToString gives the digits, which Rexx computes with under a large enough NUMERIC DIGITS. .NET's decimal has 28 digits and decimal rounding: Decimal.Divide and Decimal.Round.
See also Reference, Values.

section.title: Files and Directories
section.para: You want to read and write files, and to walk directories, in the same way on every system.

example.title: Files and Directories
example.programlisting:
io = .net~System~IO dir = io~Path~Combine(io~Path~GetTempPath, "cookbook-" || io~Path~GetRandomFileName) io~Directory~CreateDirectory(dir) file = io~Path~Combine(dir, "notes.txt") io~File~WriteAllLines(file, .array~of("first", "second", "third")) io~File~AppendAllText(file, "fourth" || .net~System~Environment~NewLine) lines = io~File~ReadAllLines(file) say lines~items "lines; the last:" lines[lines~items] info = io~FileInfo~new(file) say info~Name info~Extension (info~Length > 0) do f over io~Directory~GetFiles(dir, "*.txt") say io~Path~GetFileName(f) end io~Directory~Delete(dir, .true) say io~Directory~Exists(dir)
::requires "net.cls"
example.screen: 4 lines; the last: fourth notes.txt .txt 1 notes.txt 0

section.para: How it works. System.IO's static classes do it in one call each: File (WriteAllLines, ReadAllLines, AppendAllText), Directory, and Path, which builds paths with the system's separator. A Rexx Array goes to WriteAllLines as a string[], and ReadAllLines's string[] comes back as a Rexx-like array, from 1. A FileInfo describes a file.
See also Reference, Arrays, Collections and References.

section.title: Regular Expressions
section.para: You want regular expressions: matching, named groups, replacing, splitting.

example.title: Regular Expressions
example.programlisting:
re = .net~System~Text~RegularExpressions~Regex text = "Ann: 555-1234, Bob: 555-9876" do m over re~Matches(text, "(?<name>\w+): (?<phone>[\d-]+)") say m~Groups["name"]~Value "->" m~Groups["phone"]~Value end say re~IsMatch("2026-10-16", "^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$") say re~Replace(text, "\d{3}-(\d{4})", "XXX-$1") say re~Split("a1b22c333d", "\d+")~makeString("L", " ") say re~Replace("hello world", "\w+", .net~handler(.Upper~new, "UP"))
::requires "net.cls" ::class Upper ::method up use arg match return match~Value~upper
example.screen: Ann -> 555-1234 Bob -> 555-9876 1 Ann: XXX-1234, Bob: XXX-9876 a b c d HELLO WORLD

section.para: How it works. Regex's static methods take the pattern each time. DO m OVER re~Matches(...) walks the matches; m~Groups["name"] is a named group (the indexer takes the name). Replace takes a replacement pattern ($1), or a MatchEvaluator: a Rexx method, through a handler, which gets each match and returns its replacement.
See also Reference, Callbacks, Events and Tasks.

section.title: JSON
section.para: You want to read and write JSON.

example.title: JSON
example.programlisting:
json = '{"name": "ooRexx", "version": 5.3, "tags": ["rexx", "dotnet"], "open": true}' doc = .net~System~Text~Json~JsonDocument~Parse(json) root = doc~RootElement say root~GetProperty("name")~GetString root~GetProperty("version")~GetDouble do t over root~GetProperty("tags")~EnumerateArray say "tag:" t~GetString end say root~GetProperty("open")~ValueKind doc~Dispose d = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary<string, object>")~new d["language"] = "Rexx"; d["year"] = .net~int32(1979) opts = .net~System~Text~Json~JsonSerializerOptions~new say .net~System~Text~Json~JsonSerializer~Serialize(d)
::requires "net.cls"
example.screen: ooRexx 5.3 tag: rexx tag: dotnet True {"language":"Rexx","year":1979}

section.para: How it works. System.Text.Json reads a document as a tree of JsonElements: GetProperty, GetString, GetDouble, EnumerateArray (walked with DO OVER), ValueKind (an enum value). A JsonDocument holds pooled memory: Dispose it. JsonSerializer writes a .NET object as JSON; a Dictionary<string, object> holds what Rexx puts in it (a forced int stays a number, a Rexx string is a string).
See also Reference, Values.

section.title: Hashes, Base64 and GUIDs
section.para: You want a cryptographic hash, Base64, or a unique identifier.

example.title: Hashes, Base64 and GUIDs
example.programlisting:
bytes = .net~System~Text~Encoding~UTF8~GetBytes("hello") hash = .net~System~Security~Cryptography~SHA256~HashData(bytes) say .net~System~Convert~ToHexString(hash)~lower say .net~System~Convert~ToBase64String(bytes) say .net~System~Text~Encoding~UTF8~GetString(.net~System~Convert~FromBase64String("aGVsbG8=")) g = .net~System~Guid~NewGuid say g~ToString~length g~ToString~countStr("-")
::requires "net.cls"

section.para: How it works. Strings become bytes through an Encoding (UTF8), and bytes are a .NET array, a Rexx-like array, that goes to SHA256.HashData as it is. Convert.ToHexString and Convert.ToBase64String give text back. Guid.NewGuid is a new identifier, a struct, shown with ToString.
See also Reference, Arrays, Collections and References.
